acceptedAnswer.text: Keccak is a family of cryptographic hash functions designed by Guido Bertoni, Joan Daemen, Michaël Peeters, and Gilles Van Assche. It won the NIST hash function competition in 2012 and became the basis for SHA-3. The Keccak variants — Keccak-224, Keccak-256, Keccak-384, and Keccak-512 — use a sponge construction over a permutation-based design, differing from the Merkle–Damgård structure used by MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-2.

Keccak-256 is the hash function used natively by Ethereum for address derivation, transaction signing, and smart contract storage. It produces a 256-bit digest and is the most widely deployed member of the Keccak family. Note that Keccak-256 differs from the NIST-standardised SHA3-256 in its padding scheme.

Keccak-256 is considered secure against all known practical attacks. No collision or pre-image attack has been demonstrated against the full variant. Its sponge construction provides strong security proofs and has withstood extensive cryptanalytic scrutiny since the SHA-3 competition.

mainEntity.name: Which Keccak variant should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keccak-256 is the right default for most applications, and the only choice for Ethereum compatibility. Keccak-384 and Keccak-512 offer wider digests for higher-security contexts. Keccak-224 should only be chosen where a smaller digest size is a strict requirement.

mainEntity.name: Are Keccak hashes safe for passwords?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Keccak functions are designed to be fast, which makes them unsuitable for password storage. Use a slow, purpose-built algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 instead.

mainEntity.name: How does Keccalc protect my data?

acceptedAnswer.text: All hashing runs entirely inside your browser using hash-wasm by Daninet, a WebAssembly-accelerated library. No text, file content, or hash output is ever transmitted to any server.
